Key Characteristics & Etiology: Mucosal erosion in stomach or duodenum (> 5 mm) extending into submucosa; primary causes are Helicobacter pylori infection (~85-90% duodenal, ~70-80% gastric) and NSAID/Aspirin use.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Disruption of mucosal defense mechanisms (bicarbonate barrier, prostaglandins) by H. pylori (cytotoxin-associated gene A/CagA, vacuolating cytotoxin/VacA) or NSAIDs (COX-1 inhibition reducing protective prostaglandins), leading to acid-peptic mucosal necrosis.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Epigastric pain (duodenal: relieved by food/antacids, pain 2-3 hrs post-meal; gastric: aggravated by food, weight loss), postprandial fullness, early satiety. Red flags: hematemesis, melena, persistent vomiting, anemia, sudden acute abdomen (perforation).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: EGD (gold standard biopsy/ulcer visualization); H. pylori testing (urea breath test, stool antigen test, rapid urease biopsy test). Treatment: Triple therapy (PPI + Amoxicillin 1g BD + Clarithromycin 500mg BD for 14 days) or Bismuth quadruple therapy; stop NSAIDs.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Bleeding originating proximal to the ligament of Treitz; non-variceal (PUD, Mallory-Weiss tear, erosive gastritis, Dieulafoy lesion) vs. variceal (portal hypertension secondary to cirrhosis).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Erosion of mucosal arteries by acid-peptic ulceration or acute rupture of high-pressure submucosal esophageal/gastric varices secondary to portal venous hypertension.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Hematemesis ('coffee-ground' emesis or bright red blood), melena (black tarry stool), hematochezia (if massive rapid transit), postural hypotension, tachycardia, syncope, pallor, hypovolemic shock.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Immediate resuscitation: IV wide-bore access, IV 0.9% Normal Saline, blood transfusion (target Hb 7-8 g/dL). Variceal: IV Terlipressin/Octreotide + prophylactic IV Ceftriaxone + urgent EGD with Band Ligation (EVL) within 12h. Non-variceal: high-dose IV PPI drip + EGD dual therapy (adrenaline + clip/cautery).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Acute inflammatory disease of the pancreas; most common causes are gallstones (cholelithiasis ~40%) and heavy alcohol consumption (~30%); other causes include hypertriglyceridemia, ERCP, drugs, hypercalcemia.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Premature intra-acinar activation of zymogens (trypsinogen into trypsin), initiating autodigestion of pancreatic parenchyma, microvascular injury, fat necrosis, systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), and multiorgan dysfunction.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Severe, constant epigastric pain radiating directly to the back, relieved by leaning forward; nausea, vomiting, fever, paralytic ileus. Severe cases: Cullen sign (periumbilical ecchymosis), Grey Turner sign (flank ecchymosis), hypotension, ARDS.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Serum amylase and lipase >= 3x upper limit of normal (lipase more specific); abdominal ultrasound (gallstones); contrast-enhanced CT abdomen at 72h (necrosis/pseudocyst). Management: aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (Ringer's lactate), analgesia, enteral nutrition, ERCP if cholangitis.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Progressive, irreversible inflammatory and fibrotic disease of the pancreas leading to loss of endocrine and exocrine function; chronic alcohol abuse (> 70-80%), hereditary, tropical, or idiopathic causes.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Repeated acute injury drives pancreatic stellate cell activation, dense acinar parenchyma fibrosis, ductal strictures, intraductal stone formation, and progressive irreversible destruction of acinar and islet cells.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Recurrent or persistent severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, exocrine insufficiency (steatorrhea, foul-smelling bulky floating stools, fat-soluble vitamin A/D/E/K deficiencies), endocrine insufficiency (pancreatogenic/type 3c diabetes mellitus), weight loss.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Fecal elastase-1 (< 200 ug/g indicates exocrine insufficiency); CT/MRI/EUS showing pancreatic calcifications, ductal dilation ('chain of lakes' pattern). Treatment: Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT/Creon taken with meals), pain management, low-fat diet, insulin for diabetes.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Yellowish discoloration of skin and sclera due to serum total bilirubin > 35-50 umol/L (2-3 mg/dL); classified into pre-hepatic (unconjugated), hepatic (mixed), and post-hepatic/cholestatic (conjugated).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Pre-hepatic: excess heme breakdown (hemolysis, ineffective erythropoiesis). Hepatic: impaired hepatic uptake, conjugation (Gilbert/Crigler-Najjar), or hepatocellular secretion (hepatitis, cirrhosis). Post-hepatic: mechanical biliary tree obstruction (choledocholithiasis, pancreatic head carcinoma).
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Scleral icterus, jaundice. Cholestatic hallmarks: dark tea-colored urine, pale/clay-colored stools, intense pruritus, xanthelasma. Red flags: fever + rigor + jaundice + RUQ pain (Charcot triad for acute cholangitis; add hypotension + confusion = Reynolds pentad).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: LFTs: Cholestatic pattern (marked ALP/GGT elevation > AST/ALT); Hepatocellular pattern (marked AST/ALT elevation > ALP). Abdominal ultrasound (biliary dilation); MRCP / ERCP for obstructive ductal lesions.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Rapid-onset severe liver injury in a patient WITHOUT pre-existing cirrhosis, characterized by coagulopathy (INR > 1.5) and hepatic encephalopathy within 24 weeks of onset; paracetamol toxicity (most common), viral hepatitis (A, B, E), idiosyncratic drug reactions.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Massive hepatocyte necrosis causes acute loss of synthetic function (clotting factors, albumin), metabolic clearance failure (ammonia accumulation), systemic vasodilation, cerebral edema, hyperammonemia-mediated astrocyte swelling, and multiorgan failure.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy (Grade I: confusion/mood change; Grade II: lethargy/flapping tremor/asterixis; Grade III: stupor; Grade IV: coma), cerebral edema (increased ICP, sluggish pupils), mucosal bleeding, hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Coagulopathy (INR > 1.5, prolonged PT); elevated serum ammonia, bilirubin, transaminases; arterial lactate; hypoglycemia. Management: ICU support, N-acetylcysteine (NAC for paracetamol and non-paracetamol ALF), Lactulose/Rifaximin, mannitol/3% hypertonic saline for cerebral edema; urgent liver transplant evaluation (King's College Criteria).

Entity / Condition: Viral Hepatitis (A, B, C, D, E)
Key Characteristics & Etiology: Systemic viral infection primarily targeting hepatocytes; HAV/HEV (fecal-oral, acute only except HEV in pregnancy/immunocompromised); HBV/HCV/HDV (parenteral/sexual/vertical transmission, risk of chronicity).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Immune-mediated hepatocyte destruction (cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell attack against viral antigens on hepatocytes) leading to lobular inflammation, ballooning degeneration, Councilman bodies (apoptotic hepatocytes), and potential chronic fibrosis/cirrhosis (HBV/HCV).
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Prodrome: malaise, low-grade fever, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, myalgia, RUQ discomfort; icteric phase: jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, hepatomegaly. Chronic HBV/HCV: often asymptomatic until cirrhosis, portal hypertension, or Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) develops.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Acute HAV/HEV: IgM anti-HAV / IgM anti-HEV. HBV serology panel: HBsAg (active infection), Anti-HBs (immunity), IgM Anti-HBc (acute infection), IgG Anti-HBc (past/chronic infection), HBeAg (high replicative state/infectivity), HBV DNA. HCV: Anti-HCV screening + HCV RNA PCR. Treatment: Nucleos(t)ide analogs (Tenofovir, Entecavir) for HBV; Direct-Acting Antivirals (DAAs like Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir) for HCV (> 95% cure).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: End-stage chronic liver disease defined histologically by diffuse hepatic fibrosis and conversion of normal architecture into structurally abnormal regenerative nodules; major causes: chronic alcohol abuse, chronic HBV/HCV, MASLD/MASH.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Disruption of hepatic architecture increases intrahepatic vascular resistance, causing portal venous pressure > 10-12 mmHg (portal hypertension), splanchnic vasodilation, arterial underfilling, RAAS/ADH activation, fluid retention (ascites), and portosystemic collateral formation.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Stigmata of chronic liver disease: spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, testicular atrophy, Dupuytren contracture, caput medusae. Complications: ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), esophageal variceal bleeding, hepatic encephalopathy, hepatorenal syndrome (HRS).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Serum albumin < 35 g/L, prolonged PT/INR, thrombocytopenia (splenomegaly/hypersplenism); liver USG (nodular surface, splenomegaly, ascites); transient elastography (FibroScan). Ascites paracentesis: SAAG >= 11 g/L indicates portal hypertension; neutrophil count >= 250/mm3 diagnoses SBP (treat with IV Cefotaxime/Ceftriaxone).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Diarrhea lasting > 4 weeks; malabsorption syndromes characterized by impaired nutrient absorption across intestinal mucosa. Key causes: Celiac Disease (autoimmune gluten sensitivity), Tropical Sprue, Inflammatory Bowel Disease (Crohn's, Ulcerative Colitis), Chronic Pancreatitis.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Celiac: immune response against gliadin triggers villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis in duodenum/jejunum. Crohn's: transmural, skip lesions, non-caseating granulomas anywhere from mouth to anus. Ulcerative Colitis: continuous mucosal inflammation starting at rectum extending proximally.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Chronic watery/fatty stools (steatorrhea: bulky, pale, foul-smelling floating stools), weight loss, muscle wasting, anemia (iron deficiency in duodenal disease, B12/folate in ileal disease), metabolic bone disease (osteomalacia/osteoporosis due to vitamin D malabsorption), peripheral edema (hypoalbuminemia).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Celiac: anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) IgA + total IgA; duodenal biopsy (gold standard). IBD: fecal calprotectin (elevated), colonoscopy with biopsies (Crohn's: cobblestoning, linear ulcers, skip lesions; UC: continuous mucosal ulceration, pseudopolyps). Stool microscopy, fat quantification.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Acute infectious enteritis/colitis; Cholera (Vibrio cholerae, non-invasive secretory diarrhea); Bacillary Dysentery (Shigella spp.); Amoebic Dysentery (Entamoeba histolytica).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: V. cholerae: cholera toxin increases mucosal intracellular cAMP, driving massive active secretion of Cl- and water into gut lumen. Shigella: Shiga toxin + mucosal invasion causing acute hemorrhagic colitis. E. histolytica: trophozoite tissue invasion forming characteristic 'flask-shaped' mucosal ulcers.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Cholera: painless, massive, profuse 'rice-water' watery diarrhea (up to 1L/hr), rapid severe dehydration, hypovolemic shock, sunken eyes, muscle cramps. Dysentery: painful frequent small-volume bloody mucoid stools, severe tenesmus, high fever (Shigella), or right lobe liver abscess (Amoebic).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Stool dark-field microscopy / culture (V. cholerae); stool microscopy for E. histolytica trophozoites containing ingested RBCs or Shigella WBCs/blood. Treatment: Cholera: aggressive oral rehydration solution (ORS) or IV Ringer's lactate + Doxycycline/Azithromycin; Amoebic: Metronidazole/Tinidazole followed by luminal agent (Diloxanide furoate or Paromomycin); Shigella: Ciprofloxacin or Azithromycin.
